title: Your Parent Died With $300,000 in a Bank Account and No Beneficiary. Does All of It Have to Go Through Probate?
summary: A bank account with no beneficiary may or may not go through probate, depending on how it was owned and your state's small-estate rules.
body_markdown:
A $300,000 bank account does not always have to go through probate, even when[no beneficiary has been listed](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/what-happens-to-a-bank-account-when-someone-dies-without-a-beneficiary) . Some accounts transfer automatically at death, while others become part of the probate estate. If your parent was the sole owner and didn’t name a beneficiary, your family may have to wait for the probate process before receiving any of the money. Here is an example of what can happen to a $300,000 bank account and what you can do about it.


## How Account Ownership Determines Whether Probate Is Required


A[will can decide who inherits the money](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/have-2-million-and-simple-will-this-is-the-moment-it-stopped-being-enough) , but it does not by itself keep a solely owned account out of probate.[Probate is the court process](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/what-is-probate) that confirms a will, pays the person’s final debts and then distributes what is left. The bank generally will not release the money based on a will alone.


If the account was solely in your parent’s name, with no[payable-on-death (POD)](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/payable-on-death) beneficiary and no other automatic transfer feature, the $300,000 generally becomes part of the estate. A POD beneficiary is a person the account owner names to receive the money directly at death. Without one, the bank may need proof that a court has authorized a personal representative or executor to collect the money on behalf of the estate.


Joint accounts work differently, and the result depends on the account agreement and your state’s law.[Most joint accounts carry survivorship rights](https://smartasset.com/checking-account/joint-accounts-after-death) , which means the surviving owner automatically receives the full balance. Some do not, so it helps to ask the bank which type your parent had. The table below compares three common setups:


Account setup What generally happens at death Probate may be required?


Sole owner, no beneficiary Balance enters the estate Yes


Joint with survivorship rights Balance passes to surviving owner Usually no


POD beneficiary Balance passes to beneficiary Usually no


If your parent’s account falls into the first row, the money may be tied up until the estate is settled. A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_inheritance&utm_content=parentdiedwith300000inbankaccountandnobeneficiarydoesithavetogothroughprobate_a) can help you plan around what your family will actually have available in the meantime and what to do with the inheritance after.


## How $300,000 Could Be Distributed When There Is No Beneficiary


When the account was solely owned without a beneficiary the money becomes part of the estate and is then distributed to heirs.[With a valid will](https://smartasset.com/retirement/last-will-and-testament) , the estate generally passes according to its terms after debts, taxes and administration expenses are paid. Without a will, state intestacy law determines who inherits.


Keep in mind that actual expenses vary, so[heirs](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/heir-vs-beneficiary) generally should not treat the full balance as immediately available. For example, if the estate has debts and expenses totaling $25,000, the amount remaining for heirs would be $275,000. The table below shows how that amount could be divided among three children, with and without a surviving spouse:


Scenario Left for heirs How it is divided Each share


Will leaves equal shares to three children $275,000 Three equal shares $91,667 each


No will, no surviving spouse, three children $275,000 Equal shares under intestacy $91,667 each


No will, surviving spouse and three children (hypothetical state rule: spouse receives half) $275,000 $137,500 to the spouse, $137,500 split among the children $137,500 to the spouse, $45,833 per child


[Federal estate tax](https://smartasset.com/taxes/all-about-the-estate-tax) is unlikely to reduce these amounts, because the exemption is far larger than the account. The exemption is the amount of an estate that is shielded from federal estate tax, and only the value above that amount can be taxed. The[federal tax exemption](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/gift-tax-explained-2021-exemption-and-rates) for a parent who died in 2026 is $15 million (this limit increases to $15.48 million in 2027).1


A $300,000 account by itself is far below either federal basic exclusion amount, though federal estate tax depends on the value of the decedent’s overall estate and other relevant factors. A few states charge their own[estate or inheritance tax](https://smartasset.com/taxes/estate-tax-vs-inheritance-tax) , and some start at much lower amounts than the federal exemption. Heirs should check the rules where your parent lived to see whether their state taxes estates or inheritances.

## **Some States Offer Simpler Probate for Smaller Estates**


[Smaller estates](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/what-is-a-small-estate-affidavit) may qualify for a streamlined process instead of full probate. California, for example, allows certain personal property to transfer without full probate when the qualifying estate does not exceed $208,850 for deaths on or after April 1, 2025.2 Nevada, by comparison, allows a simpler probate process for estates worth up to $500,000. Those worth less than $150,000 may qualify for an even simpler process.3


Because these limits vary by state, a $300,000 account may require full probate in one state but qualify for a streamlined process in another. Even then, the family may still need affidavits or court documents before the bank releases the money.


Before deciding[which probate process applies](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/when-is-probate-required) , start by checking the account title and transfer instructions to see whether the money belongs in the probate estate at all. A will or an unfunded trust, meaning one the account was never moved into, does not change ownership of the account on its own.
